title: Broadcasting Internet Datagrams in the Presence of Subnets
summary: This RFC extends the broadcasting rules in RFC 919 to networks that are divided into subnets. It proposes how to address broadcasts and how gateways should handle them when subnets are present.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 922 defines how an IP host can send a datagram to all hosts on a local network, a remote network, or all subnets of a network. It also gives gateways rules for forwarding broadcasts without creating loops.

questions: how do ip broadcasts work with subnets
how to address broadcasts to a subnet
how does ip broadcast work with subnets
subtitle: Addressing and forwarding IP broadcasts when a network is divided into subnets.

tldr.problem: IP did not define a common way to broadcast, and subnetting made it unclear how a sender should identify all hosts or how gateways should forward broadcasts without loops.
tldr.mechanism: All-ones host and subnet fields identify broadcasts. Gateways avoid sending a broadcast back onto its incoming network and use Reverse Path Forwarding for broadcasts across all subnets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 922 standardizes conventions for local, directed, and multi-subnet broadcasts. The unit metadata lists no later replacement.

facts.label: All-hosts convention
facts.value: Host number with all bits one

facts.label: All-subnets convention
facts.value: Subnet number with all bits one

today: RFC 922 is an Internet Standard published in October 1984. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Networks Use Broadcasts
sections.content:
A host can broadcast when it needs information but does not know which neighbor can provide it, or when it needs to inform many hosts. This can be faster than maintaining fixed lists or trying possible host addresses one at a time.

Broadcasts are unreliable and may be duplicated. Every host that receives one must spend some effort on it, so the RFC says they should be used only when they are the best way to solve a problem.
sections.plainLanguage: A broadcast reaches many hosts without first identifying each one. Because every receiving host must process it, unnecessary broadcasts waste network resources.

sections.title: Networks and Subnets
sections.content:
A local hardware network is the physical link attached to a host. A remote hardware network is separated from it by at least one gateway. An IP network can consist of one hardware network or several connected hardware networks that share an IP network number.

A subnet is one member of a subnetted IP network. Its address divides the local portion into a subnet number and a host number. RFC 922 does not assume a particular division, and says remote hosts should not need to know whether a network contains subnets.
sections.plainLanguage: An IP network may contain one physical network or several subnets connected by gateways. The subnet and host fields identify where a host sits within that network.

sections.title: Kinds of IP Broadcast
sections.content:
A local hardware broadcast reaches hosts on the sender's physical network. A directed broadcast is routed normally until it reaches the destination network, where a gateway broadcasts it. A multi-subnet broadcast addresses all subnets in one IP network.

A datagram sent to one host may also be broadcast at the data-link layer, but that is not an IP broadcast. The RFC considers a broadcast to the entire Internet undesirable. A gateway may refuse to forward broadcasts for performance or security reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: Broadcasts can target one local network, a remote network, or every subnet in a network. A broadcast to the entire Internet is not a desirable use of the mechanism.

sections.title: Gateway Forwarding Rules
sections.content:
A host sends a local or directed broadcast by choosing the appropriate destination address and sending the datagram normally. Gateways handle the routing decisions. The primary loop-prevention rule is never to broadcast a datagram on the hardware network on which it arrived.

For a broadcast to every subnet, a gateway uses Reverse Path Forwarding. It forwards copies only when the datagram arrived on the link that is part of the best route back to its source; otherwise it discards the datagram as a duplicate.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway must not rebroadcast a datagram onto the network where it arrived. For an all-subnets broadcast, it forwards only when the incoming link is on the best route back to the source.

sections.title: Broadcast Address Conventions
sections.content:
The RFC uses all-ones values for the host number meaning all hosts and the subnet number meaning all subnets. This lets a sender address all hosts in an IP network without knowing how the address is divided or whether the network is subnetted.

255.255.255.255 means a broadcast on the local hardware network and must not be forwarded. For example, 36.255.255.255 means all hosts on network 36. All-zero fields are used as a notation for the network itself, such as 36.0.0.0.
sections.plainLanguage: An all-ones host field means all hosts, and an all-ones subnet field means all subnets. The address 255.255.255.255 stays on the local network and is not forwarded.

sections.title: ARP and Broadcast Loops
sections.content:
An Address Resolution Protocol server must not answer a request whose target is an IP broadcast address. A host that asks for such a mapping does not recognize the address as a broadcast; providing a hardware broadcast address can create a forwarding loop.

The RFC warns that such loops can multiply broadcasts. Gateways may also block broadcast forwarding for security or performance reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: An ARP server must not map a broadcast IP address to a hardware broadcast address. That answer can cause repeated forwarding and multiply traffic.

items.label: Local broadcast
items.desc: Broadcast on the local hardware network; it must not be forwarded.

items.label: Network 36 broadcast
items.desc: All hosts on network 36, whether or not it is subnetted.
